<reason>Both sides were disciplined and well-written, but B controlled the decisive question. From B2.7 onward, B pressed a clean dilemma: everything A proposed to make the bargaining table safe (mandated seats, public veto, limited product) is legislation, so a constrained table is "a statute wearing a bargaining label" and the motion adds nothing; unconstrained, it adds only insider authorship binding non-members. A never squarely answered what bargaining uniquely contributes beyond statute-plus-consultation — A's answer was to add more statutory constraints, which fed B's frame. A landed one real hit in the closing: B's acceptance of industry-specific statutory floors means B's signature exclusion harm is common to both worlds. That partially neutralized B's offense, but B's core objection was comparative about mechanism (public authorship vs. insider deals with extension power), not about whether floors should exist, and B5 answered A's late "statutes can't reach fissured work" claim with joint-liability/supply-chain legislation. B also answered pressure questions more cleanly: its "yes" to industry floors was pre-committed in B1.6 and turned into proof of the statute/bargaining distinction, while A's honest "nothing reconnects her" conceded the human cost. A's clipped Rebuttal 1 was a real but modest execution cost. B made the debate easier to decide.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>B4.2 completing the trap set by B2.7: every safeguard A listed to make the table safe is legislation — "strip away the bargaining and nothing of value is lost; keep it and you add exactly one thing: insider authorship with the force of law." A never escaped that dilemma.</best_rebuttal>
